overview: Taylor Wimpey is one of the UK's largest homebuilders, operating at a local level from 22 regional businesses organised into five divisions across England, Scotland and Wales, with a smaller second-homes operation in Spain. The Group buys land, takes it through the planning system, and builds and sells private and affordable new homes, generating revenue almost entirely from completed home sales (UK Group completions of 11,229 including joint ventures in FY2025; revenue of £3,844.6m). It is a cyclical, capital-intensive business whose profitability is highly sensitive to mortgage rates, consumer affordability, land and build cost inflation, and the planning environment.

business_model.summary: Taylor Wimpey buys short-term (planning-ready) and strategic (pre-planning) land, develops it through the planning system, builds homes using a mix of directly employed site teams and subcontracted labour, and sells completed homes to private buyers, affordable/registered housing providers (via Section 106 obligations) and occasionally bulk/institutional buyers. Revenue is transactional and project-based (recognised on legal completion of each home), not recurring, though the order book (c.6,900 UK homes worth c.£1.9bn as of H1 2026) gives several months of forward revenue visibility. Profitability is a function of land cost as a percentage of ASP (c.12.5-13.8% on the current landbank/approvals), build cost inflation, pricing/incentives, and overhead control. A small, higher-margin Spanish second-homes business (c.5% of Group revenue, ~26-27% operating margin vs ~10% in the UK) sells predominantly to European/international buyers.

revenue_streams.name: Spain (second homes)
revenue_streams.trend: normalizing lower after two elevated years

revenue_streams.name: Joint ventures (share of profit, off-balance-sheet revenue)

business_model.customer_type: B2C (private homebuyers, predominantly first-time buyers and second/next-steppers) plus B2B/B2G (registered social landlords and Local Authorities for affordable housing, and occasional bulk/institutional buyers)
business_model.geographic_mix: UK ~95% of Group revenue (London & South East, Midlands & Wales, North West & Yorkshire, Scotland/North East/North Yorkshire, Central & South West); Spain ~5% (second-home/holiday market for European and international buyers)

competitive_position.market_position: One of the UK's largest private and affordable homebuilders by volume (top 3-5 by completions), but the new-build sector itself is a small share of total UK housing transactions (c.6.4% in 2025, below the 7.8% five-year average), meaning pricing is set by the much larger second-hand market rather than by new-build competitive dynamics alone.

moat_factors.description: c.75-77k short-term owned/controlled plots plus c.132-133k strategic pipeline plots (total potential revenue c.£60bn) built up over decades via option agreements, giving multi-year visibility and negotiating leverage with land vendors that smaller builders lack.

Long-dated relationships with Local Authorities and a track record of converting strategic (non-planning) land into consented land at a discount to market value; management cites 'the most positive planning outlook since 2012.'

Net cash position (£168.6m at H1 2026, guided to c.£250m at FY2026 year-end) and £686m of committed facilities (£600m RCF undrawn) allow it to weather downturns and be selective on land purchases when smaller/leveraged competitors cannot.

Five-star HBF builder status and sector-leading Construction Quality Review (CQR) scores support premium positioning and lower warranty/remediation risk versus some peers, though this is a reputational rather than structural moat.

moat_factors.factor: Economies of scale in procurement and standardisation
moat_factors.description: National framework supplier agreements, in-house timber frame manufacturing (Taylor Wimpey Manufacturing) and standard house types reduce unit costs versus smaller regional builders, but do not differentiate materially versus similarly sized peers (Barratt Redrow, Persimmon, Vistry).

weaknesses: No pricing power: new-build pricing is dictated by the much larger second-hand housing market, limiting the ability to pass through build cost and regulatory cost inflation
High fixed/semi-fixed cost base (22 regional businesses, WIP cycle of c.9 months) makes margins highly operationally geared to volume swings
Reliance on mortgage-dependent, often first-time-buyer customers who are the most affordability-constrained segment
Spain, while higher-margin, is a small, non-diversifying, discretionary second-homes market with its own volume volatility (completions nearly halved H1 2026 vs H1 2025)
Legacy building-safety/cladding liabilities create an open-ended cost and reputational overhang versus purely greenfield-focused smaller builders

growth_drivers: Outlet growth: average UK outlets up 6% YoY to 219 in H1 2026 (209 at FY2025, targeting continued growth into the medium term) as planning conditions improve
Most favourable UK planning backdrop since 2012: revised NPPF (Dec 2024), Planning and Infrastructure Act (law Dec 2025) streamlining decision-making and limiting judicial review delays
Strategic land pipeline conversion (c.132-133k potential plots) allows outlet/volume growth largely without net new land investment, improving capital efficiency/asset turn

Medium-term targets set at October 2025 Investor Day: c.14k UK completions (ex-JV), landbank years reduced to 4.5-5.0 (from c.7.0-7.2), Group adjusted operating profit margin of 16-18% and return on net operating assets of >20%
Structural UK housing undersupply (CPS-estimated 6.5m home shortfall; population growth continuing to outpace net additional dwellings) underpins long-term demand once affordability recovers
Prospect of further Bank of England rate cuts easing mortgage affordability and unlocking pent-up first-time-buyer demand
Potential Government demand-side support (equity loan scheme, Stamp Duty relief for first-time buyers) that Taylor Wimpey and the HBF are actively lobbying for
Capital recycling into smaller, higher-returning sites, improving net operating asset turn (1.01x) and freeing capital from larger, slower-turning developments

business.risk: UK housing market cyclicality / demand downturn
business.description: Net private sales rate has fallen in five straight reporting periods and was 0.55 per outlet per week in the four weeks to 26 July 2026 (vs 0.59 prior year); management now describes a 'prolonged' downturn and has cut FY2026 UK completions guidance to 10,600-10,800 (within the lower half of the March range).

business.risk: Second-hand market competition for buyer attention
business.description: Decade-high levels of second-hand stock for sale are giving buyers more choice, lengthening the sales cycle and increasing the number of appointments needed per reservation.
First-time buyers, who need the highest loan-to-value mortgages, are the most affordability-sensitive segment and a core part of Taylor Wimpey's customer base.
FY2025 gross profit absorbed an unexpected £20m charge for historical defective workmanship by a principal contractor on a London development; remediation at that site continues.

financial.risk: Land cost inflation and land as % of ASP
financial.description: Land cost as a percentage of ASP on approvals, while improved to 13.8% in H1 2026 (from 17.4% in H1 2025) as the company targets smaller, higher-returning sites, remains a key margin driver that can move adversely if land competition returns before pricing recovers.

financial.risk: Build cost inflation outpacing selling prices
financial.description: FY2026 guidance is for 3-4% build cost inflation against blended UK ASP growth of only c.1% and underlying pricing currently running c.2% below prior-year levels; this margin-cost mismatch has already driven adjusted operating margin down to 7.7% in H1 2026 from 9.7% in H1 2025 and 10.9% for FY2025.

The Board cut the annual Distribution Policy from 7.5% of net assets to 4% of net assets in July 2026 (interim dividend cut to 1.20p), reflecting lower expected profitability and cash generation through the prolonged downturn; shares fell on the announcement and the cut signals constrained capital-return capacity until the cycle turns.

financial.risk: Net cash erosion and cladding cash outflows
financial.description: Net cash fell to £168.6m at H1 2026 from £342.6m at FY2025 year-end, partly reflecting cladding-related cash outflows (c.£100m guided for FY2026, weighted to H2) plus dividends and buybacks; FY2026 year-end net cash is guided at only c.£250m.

The Taylor Wimpey Pension Scheme is in IAS19 surplus (£102.7m at H1 2026) but a notional balance-sheet deficit is recognised under IFRIC 14 because the surplus cannot be recovered by the Group; the Pension Funding Partnership has contingent payments of up to £12.5m/year from 2029-2035 if a Technical Provisions deficit re-emerges.

regulatory.risk: Building Safety Act / cladding fire-safety remediation
regulatory.description: Following Grenfell, Taylor Wimpey has recognised cumulative fire-safety provisions running into the hundreds of millions of pounds; FY2025 alone saw a £225.8m net increase (net of discounting) and H1 2026 included a £222.2m increase disclosed as an exceptional charge in the H1 2025 comparative. Provisions stood at £437.7m at H1 2026 (£492.1m at FY2025 year-end). 97% of in-scope England buildings have a remediation determination and work has started on almost half of those requiring it, but the ultimate cost and timing of full remediation (including Scotland's Developer Remediation Contract signed March 2026) remains uncertain and subject to re-estimation (cost inflation, discount-rate unwind, scope changes).

regulatory.risk: CMA information-sharing investigation / affordable housing contribution
regulatory.description: Taylor Wimpey was one of eight major UK housebuilders investigated by the CMA over alleged exchange of commercially sensitive information (pricing, incentives, viewing numbers); the case closed via voluntary commitments (no infringement finding) including a combined £100m industry contribution to the Affordable Homes Programme, of which Taylor Wimpey's share was c.£15.8-18.0m, recognised as an exceptional charge in 2025.

regulatory.risk: Future Homes Standard / Building Regulations changes
regulatory.description: New Building Regulations and transition arrangements for the Future Homes Standard were published in March 2026; compliant home designs depend on Government software (Home Energy Model) not yet released, creating specification and cost uncertainty, with the Government's cumulative regulatory changes since 2020 estimated by the HBF to have added c.£76k (c.£98k in London) to the cost of building a home.

The new Building Safety Levy is expected to take effect from October 2026, adding a further cost to new and existing land assets; Taylor Wimpey has been pricing the Levy into new land acquisitions for the past year and has used Initial Notice submissions to defer BSL liability on existing/pipeline sites until 2029.

While the revised NPPF (Dec 2024) and Planning and Infrastructure Act (law Dec 2025) are currently supportive, planning policy has shifted materially across six revisions since 2012 and a further NPPF re-write consultation opened in December 2025; local election outcomes have already introduced 'friction' in some planning decisions.

regulatory.risk: Mandatory housing targets / Government demand-support dependency
regulatory.description: Sector output (and Taylor Wimpey's own volumes) is exposed to whether Government follows through on demand-side measures (equity loans, Stamp Duty relief for first-time buyers, affordable housing funding); management has explicitly warned that without such action, 'weaker demand, rising costs and limited affordable housing funding risk reducing sector output and UK economic growth.'

macro.description: Despite four BoE base rate cuts in 2025 (to 3.75%) and average 5-year 75% LTV mortgage rates falling to 4.0% by December 2025, affordability remains stretched, particularly for first-time buyers and in the South of England; H1 2026 saw 'higher mortgage rates further stretched affordability' versus the prior year, directly compressing sales rates and ASPs.

Management explicitly cited Middle East conflict and UK political instability as having increased the inherent/residual risk on the 'Mortgage availability and housing demand' Principal Risk since the 2025 year-end, and as a factor behind the July 2026 distribution policy cut.

Housing market activity softened in H2 2025 in part due to uncertainty ahead of the UK Budget (26 November 2025), illustrating the sector's sensitivity to fiscal policy announcements (e.g., stamp duty, property taxation) even absent a specific housing measure.

Principal Risk 'Availability and costs of materials and subcontractors' was flagged as having an increased inherent risk profile since the 2025 year-end, reflecting increased supplier surcharge activity amid full-year build cost inflation guided at 3-4%.

UK unemployment rose to 5.2% (Q4 2025) from 4.4% a year earlier; a further deterioration in the labour market would compound mortgage-driven affordability pressure on an already price-conscious buyer base.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: UK new-build housing remains structurally undersupplied (CPS estimates a 6.5m home shortfall; government target of 300k homes/year vs 209k net additional dwellings delivered in England FY2024-25) but cyclically weak: new-build completions were only c.6.4% of UK housing transactions in 2025 (below the 7.8% five-year average) as elevated second-hand stock and stretched affordability diverted demand. Planning reform (NPPF, Planning and Infrastructure Act) is the most supportive since 2012 but takes years to convert into delivered homes.
macro_factors.cyclicality: High - homebuilding is one of the most cyclical sectors, driven by interest rates, consumer confidence, employment and credit availability; Taylor Wimpey's own order book, sales rate and margin have deteriorated through 2025-2026 in what management calls a 'prolonged' downturn, prompting a distribution policy cut.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Very high - mortgage rates are the single biggest driver of affordability and sales rates; BoE base rate cuts through 2025 (4.75% to 3.75%) have only partially offset affordability pressure, and further cuts are a key catalyst for demand recovery, with a lag of several months before order-book improvements convert into completions.

recent_developments.event: H1 2026 results: adjusted operating profit fell 19.4% to £129.7m on revenue up 1.7% to £1,683.0m; adjusted operating margin fell to 7.7% (H1 2025: 9.7%); net private sales rate fell to 0.75 (H1 2025: 0.79). Board cut the annual Distribution Policy from 7.5% to 4% of net assets, declared a reduced 1.20p interim dividend and announced a £42m share buyback; shares fell c.4-5% on the day.

Four-week trading update to 26 July 2026 showed net private sales rate slowing further to 0.55 per outlet per week (2025: 0.59) with underlying pricing c.2% below prior-year levels, reflecting a 'more challenging second quarter' amid increased geopolitical uncertainty (Middle East) and continued affordability constraints.

Government published Building Regulations and transition arrangements for the Future Homes Standard; Taylor Wimpey continues to await the Home Energy Model software needed to finalise compliant house designs.
Taylor Wimpey signed the Scottish Government's Developer Remediation Contract for cladding/fire-safety works, extending its remediation commitments beyond England and Wales.

UK Planning and Infrastructure Act became law, introducing a national scheme of delegation for planning decisions and limiting judicial reviews for major housing/infrastructure projects, intended to speed up planning approvals.

Investor and Analyst Day: management set new medium-term (3-5 year) targets - c.14k UK completions ex-JV, landbank years of 4.5-5.0, Group adjusted operating profit margin of 16-18% and return on net operating assets of >20% - alongside a strategy to grow outlets and recycle capital into smaller sites without net land investment.

CMA closed its multi-housebuilder information-sharing investigation (Taylor Wimpey one of eight firms, including Barratt, Bellway, Berkeley, Persimmon, Vistry, Redrow, Bloor) via voluntary commitments with no infringement finding; firms collectively contributed £100m to the Affordable Homes Programme, with Taylor Wimpey's share c.£15.8-18.0m recognised as an exceptional charge.

FY2025 results: revenue £3,844.6m (2024: £3,401.2m), adjusted operating profit £420.6m (margin 10.9%, down from 12.2%), but statutory profit before tax fell sharply to £146.5m (2024: £320.3m) after £243.8m of exceptional charges, dominated by a £225.8m net increase in the cladding fire-safety provision. Full-year ordinary dividend cut to 7.62p (2024: 9.46p); net cash fell to £342.6m (2024: £564.8m).

Sell-side price target reductions through 2026: Citigroup cut target to 105p (maintained Buy), Deutsche Bank cut to 82p (Hold), Berenberg cut to 95p (Buy), JPMorgan Underweight at 70p; consensus moved from a c.126p average target in January 2026 to roughly 85-99p by August 2026, alongside director (Mark Castle) share purchases around 75p.

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Jennie Daly described H1 2026 as 'a solid first half performance in a challenging market' but acknowledged 'continuing market uncertainty in which affordability remains stretched' and that the housing downturn 'has proved more prolonged than anticipated.' She flagged rising build costs and regulatory costs as making it 'harder to build in the places where homes are needed most' and called for Government action on demand-side measures (equity loan scheme, Stamp Duty relief for first-time buyers) and a moratorium on further regulation. Management reiterated confidence in the medium-term targets set at the October 2025 Investor Day, contingent on market conditions normalising, and emphasised continued tight control of WIP (down 6% per outlet YoY), cost discipline and outlet growth (228 outlets at H1 2026 vs 209 a year earlier) as the levers within its control during the downturn.

bull_case: Structural UK housing undersupply (6.5m home deficit per CPS) and the most favourable planning backdrop since 2012 (NPPF revision, Planning and Infrastructure Act) set up a strong multi-year volume recovery once affordability improves

Strong balance sheet (net cash, £600m undrawn RCF, no debt covenant stress) allows Taylor Wimpey to keep investing in outlets and land selectively while financially weaker competitors are forced to retrench, positioning it to gain share coming out of the downturn

Large, high-quality, low-cost-basis landbank (land at only 12.5% of ASP) and strategic pipeline (c.132k plots) support margin recovery toward the 16-18% medium-term target without needing material new land investment

Capital efficiency initiatives (recycling into smaller sites, reducing landbank years from c.7.2 to a 4.5-5.0 target) should materially lift return on net operating assets from 11% toward the >20% medium-term target, a re-rating catalyst if delivered

Potential interest-rate cuts and/or targeted Government demand-side support (stamp duty relief, equity loans) could unlock meaningful pent-up first-time-buyer demand given current depressed sales rates

Sell-side still carries 'Buy' ratings from several brokers (Citigroup, Berenberg) despite target cuts, implying material perceived upside from depressed 2026 trading levels (c.75-80p) to target prices in the 95-137p range
bear_case: The downturn has proved more prolonged and deeper than management or the market expected, evidenced by five consecutive periods of declining sales rates and a guidance cut to the lower half of the FY2026 completions range

Structural margin squeeze: build cost inflation (3-4%) is running well ahead of blended selling price growth (c.1%) and underlying prices remain c.2% below prior-year levels, with no clear catalyst for near-term pricing power given new-build's small share of a second-hand-dominated market

Open-ended fire-safety/cladding liability: provisions have already absorbed hundreds of millions of pounds (£225.8m net increase in FY2025 alone) with continued cash outflows guided at c.£100m in FY2026, and scope/cost estimates have proven to re-escalate as assessments evolve (e.g., cavity-barrier defects found via more invasive inspection)

The July 2026 distribution policy cut (7.5% to 4% of net assets) signals management's own reduced confidence in near-term cash generation and removes a key support for the income-investor shareholder base, which likely contributed to the share price decline

Mounting regulatory cost burden (Future Homes Standard, Building Safety Levy from October 2026, HBF-estimated c.£76-98k of added cost per home since 2020) continues to erode housebuilder economics regardless of demand conditions, and is a risk that persists even if rates fall

Mortgage affordability remains structurally stretched for the core first-time-buyer segment even after four 2025 rate cuts, and a weakening labour market (unemployment up to 5.2%) and geopolitical uncertainty add further downside risk to the demand recovery thesis
